newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court considers candidate drug test law.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court considers candidate drug test law.

text.p: The Supreme Court heard arguments Tuesday on whether a state may require that candidates for top political, legislative and judicial offices pass drug tests before they can get on the ballot.

The high court considered a 1990 Georgia law that requires drug tests for candidates for governor, lieutenant governor, secretary of state, attorney general, heads of several agencies, state judges and state legislators. Under the law, anyone who declines to take the test or who tests positive is barred from holding office.

The lawyer challenging the law argued that the urinalysis test for five illegal drugs violates constitutional privacy rights and said the state had offered no evidence that government officials have a problem with drug abuse.
But an attorney for the state replied that voters have a right to know that candidates for office were drug-free and cited a long line of Supreme Court rulings that upheld mandatory drug tests.

Walker Chandler, a Libertarian Party member who ran unsuccessfully for lieutenant governor in 1994, was among those who challenged the law. Arguing the case before the high court, he said the drug tests violate the constitutional right to be free from unreasonable searches and seizures and amount to an improper expansion of government power for what he called a merely symbolic purpose.
"There is no real evidence of a real problem" involving drug abusers in office," he said, claiming the state had failed to offer any justification for the tests.
But he ran into problems when the justices asked about other hypothetical situations.
Justice Sandra Day O'Connor asked whether the state instead could require that every candidate for office file an affidavit certifying the individual has not used illegal drugs.
"I would object to that," Chandler answered.
But O'Connor pressed on, saying there would be no search and that the state has wide powers in defining the qualifications for state office.
Chief Justice William Rehnquist asked whether candidates could be required to take a drug test but could then get on the ballot after the results were announced.

Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg asked if a state could require a drug test once a year after an official had been elected. Chandler said he would oppose that as well because "blanket searches are intolerable."
But when pressed by Justice Anthony Kennedy on whether drug use in office was irrelevant, Chandler acknowledged it would depend on the frequency and the drugs involved.

Georgia Assistant Attorney General Patricia Guilday also faced tough questions while defending the law. She admitted there was no evidence in the record that Georgia has a problem with state officials abusing drugs but said elected officials were "servants of the public" and must be "held to a higher standard."

Justice Stephen Breyer noted the drug test was required within a certain time period for each candidate, which was known in advance. "The greatest druggie could find a day when he was drug free," he said, adding that random tests would offer a better chance of catching drug abusers.
A ruling in the case is expected by the end of June.
